name: Nabal
charge: Churlish refusal of hospitality; railing on the Lord's anointed
summary: David's men had guarded Nabal's shepherds all season. At sheep-shearing David asked for provision; Nabal, churlish and evil in his doings, answered, who is David? and sent them away. Abigail's wisdom stopped David's sword. The Lord did not stop his own.
offense: Nabal possessed three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. At sheep-shearing David sent a peaceful request for provision, reminding him that his shepherds and goods had been safe among David's men (1 Samuel 25:2-9). Nabal's own servant confirmed their conduct: they had been a wall by night and day, and nothing had gone missing (1 Samuel 25:14-16). The benefit was known within the household before the request arrived. Nabal answered with contempt, asking who David was and comparing him to a servant breaking away from his master. He would not give his bread, water, and meat to these men (1 Samuel 25:10-11). His repeated claim upon his possessions ignored the protection through which he had enjoyed them. Wealth had become the reason to close his hand rather than the means to supply a need. His servant described him as a man who could not be reasoned with (1 Samuel 25:17). That spirit made correction difficult before the danger arrived. Deuteronomy 15:7-11 forbids hardening the heart and shutting the hand against a needy brother. Nabal joined refusal to railing, repaying good with evil while his household prepared to feast.
judgment: David armed four hundred men and intended to destroy the males of the household. Abigail intervened with provision and counsel, keeping him from avenging himself by bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:13, 18-35). Nabal's guilt did not authorize every act David's anger proposed. The Lord's restraint of David was mercy toward his servant and those his sword would have struck.

entries.commentary: Samuel died, and all the Israelites gathered together and lamented him and buried him in his house at Ramah; and David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran. There was a very great man in Maon whose possessions were in Carmel, three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, shearing his sheep in Carmel. His name was Nabal, and his wife was Abigail, a woman of good understanding and of a beautiful countenance; but the man was churlish and evil in his doings, and he was of the house of Caleb.

David heard in the wilderness that Nabal did shear his sheep and sent ten young men to greet him in peace: peace be to thee, to thine house, and to all that thou hast. The request was righteous: thy shepherds were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them all the while they were in Carmel; ask thy young men and they will shew thee. We come in a good day; give whatsoever cometh to thine hand unto thy servants and to thy son David.

Nabal answered, Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master. He was talking much smack, as if he did not even know who David was, and refused to give of his bread, his water, and his flesh to men he knew not. When his young men told David, he said, Gird ye on every man his sword; about four hundred men went up after David, and two hundred abode by the stuff.

One of the young men told Abigail: David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master, and he railed on them. But the men were very good unto us; we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing as long as we were conversant with them; they were a wall unto us both by night and day while we were keeping the sheep. David's men had been giving Nabal's shepherds protection from their enemies. Evil is determined against our master and against all his household, for he is such a son of Belial that a man cannot speak to him. Some of us know people like that: you cannot talk to them, they will not reason with you. Consider that Nabal was rich, a very wealthy man, and a lot of times what comes with that is an arrogant spirit.

Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, clusters of raisins, and cakes of figs, laid them on asses, and sent her servants on before her; but she told not her husband Nabal. David had said, Surely in vain have I kept all that this fellow hath in the wilderness; he hath requited me evil for good. He swore to leave Nabal none by the morning light of any that pisseth against the wall; David was coming with intent to destroy the men of that house.

When Abigail saw David she hasted, lighted off the ass, fell at his feet, and said, Upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be. She was not the one who did anything wrong, but she took that iniquity upon herself; she was being that pillar of her house, using wisdom to protect it, for the scripture says she was a woman of good understanding. She did not turn her lord over to be destroyed, as some women today would be ready to do; instead she pleaded, Let not my lord regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. She had not seen the young men David sent, or she would have stepped in then to protect their house.

Abigail said, The Lord hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood and from avenging thyself with thine own hand; now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal. She asked, Forgive the trespass of thine handmaid; it was Nabal who was out of the spirit, but again that chaste conversation, stepping up for her household. The soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord thy God, and the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out as out of the middle of a sling. When the Lord shall have appointed thee ruler over Israel, this shall be no grief unto thee, that thou hast shed blood causeless or that my lord hath avenged himself; then remember thine handmaid.

David said, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me, and blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood and from avenging myself with mine own hand. David received of her hand that which she had brought him and said, Go up in peace to thine house; see, I have hearkened to thy voice and have accepted thy person.

Abigail came home and Nabal held a feast in his house like the feast of a king, and his heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken; so she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light. In the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. Remember he had railed, Who is David? but when he sobered up and heard that the coming king had come down to destroy everybody in his house, his heart died within him. About ten days after, the Lord smote Nabal, that he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, Blessed be the Lord, that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and hath kept his servant from evil: for the Lord hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head. Then David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife. Abigail bowed herself on her face to the earth and said, Behold, let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord, and she arose and washed the feet of the servants who delivered the good tidings; that is a very humble act. She was probably very joyous and glad to go: a woman living with a man who is hard to deal with, who will not listen, will not take advice, arrogant, maybe verbally abusive, was relieved of that thing when Nabal died, and she hasted and arose with five damsels of hers and became David's wife.
David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and they were also both of them his wives; but Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Phalti the son of Laish, which was of Gallim.

At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release: every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it, and shall not exact it of his neighbour or of his brother, because it is called the Lord's release. Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again, but that which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release. The seven year release stands on the sabbath of the land already given in [Leviticus 25](/bible/leviticus/25).

If thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the Most High to observe all these commandments, thou shalt lend unto many nations but thou shalt not borrow, and thou shalt reign over many nations but they shall not reign over thee. This is the blessing that was to come upon us. Since we broke the commandments of the Most High, the other nations lend to us and we borrow from them; we go to them for loans and everything else.

If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren, thou shalt not harden thine heart nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother. It is a commandment to us to help our brothers: open thine hand wide unto him and lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.

Beware that there be not a thought in thy wicked heart saying, The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand, and thine eye be evil against thy poor brother and thou givest him nought; if he cry unto the Lord against thee, it is sin unto thee. Give him surely, and let not thine heart be grieved when thou givest, for because of this thing the Most High shall bless thee in all thy works. Notice that Esau had this Bible, these commandments and these laws, yet worked us to death for over four hundred years, and when they released us we did not go out with anything. They had these laws written before them and did not do them. The poor shall never cease out of the land; Christ said the same, that the poor are always going to be among us. That is why no campaign can fight poverty out of existence: Christ said it will always be among us.

If thy brother, an Hebrew man or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee and serve thee six years, then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free, and thou shalt not let him go away empty. When people say slavery was taking place in Africa among us, it was not slavery like we suffered: it was people among us that fell poor and sold themselves to their brothers, the very case this law and [Leviticus 25](/bible/leviticus/25) govern. Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress; he must leave blessed, with some of the flock, the corn, and the wine. He cannot go out poor the way he came in; that shows you the Most High is a good God. The reason given is memory: remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee.

If the servant say, I will not go away from thee, because he loveth thee and thine house and is well with thee, then thou shalt take an aul and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever; likewise unto thy maidservant. It shall not seem hard unto thee when thou sendest him away free, for he hath been worth a double hired servant to thee in serving thee six years. A double hired servant: reading this makes you think about slavery and how many years they had us. We were double hired servants unto them, and we still serve them even to this day.

All the firstling males of thy herd and of thy flock thou shalt sanctify unto the Most High: thou shalt do no work with the firstling of thy bullock, nor shear the firstling of thy sheep. The firstlings were to do no work at all; they were to be sacrificed to the Most High, and thou shalt eat it before the Lord thy God year by year in the place which the Lord shall choose. If there be any blemish therein, as if it be lame or blind, thou shalt not sacrifice it unto the Lord thy God; thou shalt eat it within thy gates, the unclean and the clean person alike, as the roebuck and as the hart. Only thou shalt not eat the blood thereof; thou shalt pour it upon the ground as water.

verses.text: And there was a man in Maon, whose possessions were in Carmel; and the man was very great, and he had three thousand sheep, and a thousand goats: and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.

Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb.
And Nabal answered David’s servants, and said, Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master.
Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?
But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying, Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master; and he railed on them.
But the men were very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields:
They were a wall unto us both by night and day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.
Now therefore know and consider what thou wilt do; for evil is determined against our master, and against all his household: for he is such a son of Belial, that a man cannot speak to him.

Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send.

And Abigail came to Nabal; and, behold, he held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king; and Nabal’s heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken: wherefore she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light.
But it came to pass in the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, and his wife had told him these things, that his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.
And it came to pass about ten days after, that the Lord smote Nabal, that he died.

And when David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, Blessed be the Lord, that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and hath kept his servant from evil: for the Lord hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head. And David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife.

If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother:
But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.

lawsResolved.text: Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some have entertained angels without knowing it.
Do not harden your heart towards the poor but lend to him sufficient to cover his need.
We are exhorted to be courteous.
Avenge not yourselves, for vengeance is in God's hands.
